extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — general educated public, scientists, reformers, and members of intellectual clubs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying evaluative criteria from popular-science essays on metric reform, the pain of drowning, and science's role in mental improvement. The page offers prescriptive principles, evidentiary standards, and procedural recommendations aimed at public audiences and scientific-minded clubs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon elaborate metric nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire abandonment of the present elaborate and ingenious system of nomenclature, and of any attempt at universality in the words employed to designate the units of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: long learned names are 'too pretty for use' and fail to gain currency; instead use plain names accessible to children, servants, and the unlearned. The page argues these lofty names have been 'stifled by general neglect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vernacular expressions for unit names
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of each unit by each nation in its own vernacular tongue — the units themselves being the same everywhere, but the expression in language adapted to the familiar tongue of each people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units remain universal in measure, but spoken names should be national/familiar to reduce friction in adoption. Example idea: prefer Anglo-Saxon short, terse, significant words when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a common written notation for universality
rubrics_metrics.description: A common notation as the means of universality, instead of a common system of names, the units and their written expression being thus universally the same, while the spoken expression conforms to familiar national usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested symbolic base-unit notations that address the eye and are self-explanatory (e.g., straight graduated line for length, square for surface, cube for solid, cup for capacity, pound-weight symbol for weight, coin for money, angle for angle, waving line for time). Emphasises notation as the practical route to international uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose unit names suggestive of familiar objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The words selected to express the several units to be suggestive of easy standards of comparison with familiar objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names should provide easy, intuitive standards of comparison (e.g., 'ten hairs' idea for millimetre) to preserve everyday familiarity and reduce learning cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make notation visually suggestive and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation also to be suggestive to the eye, as the nomenclature heretofore in use was to the learned ear, but not to the unlearned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation should be explanatory at a glance for non-experts; contrast between the difficulty of universal spoken names and the ease of universal symbols for the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce number of denominations and simplify oral expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of denominations to be reduced in conformity with an observed tendency among men to use numbers instead; oral expression to be simplified; and a suitable actual system of notation suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: collapse many intermediate units (suggested scales like 'hairs, nails, yards, kiles') so people use numeric multiples more than many special names; goal is to minimize cognitive load and simplify everyday usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transition minimizes loss of familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition to the new system to involve the least practicable loss of familiarity — either with familiar objects or familiar names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation principle: conserve familiar standards and names where possible; adapt the system to human habits rather than expecting people to adapt wholly to the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain, short, nationally-familiar names in adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Furnish users with familiar standards of comparison for units left, and give English names to boot — Anglo-Saxon when possible, short, terse, and significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: reach the mother-tongue of each people; avoid Greek/Latin/French long words and 'queer pronunciations' that impede popular adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use survivor testimony as evidence on subjective pain in drowning
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who have been resuscitated, after having become unconscious, declare that they have felt no pain whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page treats such first-hand reports as strong evidence (weighty because survivors could not plausibly forget extreme distress), and uses them to argue that drowning can be painless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider rapidity of death when assessing pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is speedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid unconsciousness or death reduces the opportunity for prolonged physical suffering; thus shorter time to unconsciousness supports the conclusion of little or no pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for mental state and its masking of physical pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who lose presence of mind are so occupied with frantic struggles and mental agony that slight physical pain would be unnoticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mental agony/terror from physical pain; evaluate whether subjective reports conflate or separate these experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess physiological mechanism producing unconsciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The entrance of water into the lungs causes powerful contraction of capillaries and obstructs pulmonary circulation, tending to produce rapid unconsciousness before the agony of asphyxia is felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physiological reasoning and comparative timing (holding breath voluntarily vs. involuntary inspiration with water) to infer whether drowning produces fast insensibility. Cite comparisons like performers holding breath for minutes vs. involuntary water aspiration causing quicker unconsciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify modes of drowning death to evaluate likely pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Drowning persons die in different ways: (1) by syncope and asphyxia while unconscious; (2) by apoplexy (congestive) followed by asphyxia while unconscious; (3) by pure and simple asphyxia. Deaths under first two are rapid and painless and constitute a large fraction of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classification to estimate proportions of painful vs. painless cases; follow cited authorities (e.g., Taylor) and observed phenomena to support probabilistic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare voluntary breath-holding durations to drowning timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people can hold their breath ~1–1.5 minutes; exceptional performers longer; but if a person's head is under water and he does not hold his breath, unconsciousness usually comes in one or two minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical timing of breath-holding and unconsciousness is used as a criterion to judge how quickly drowning leads to insensibility and thereby to infer the degree of pain experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical methods to minimize suffering in inevitable drowning
rubrics_metrics.description: If death by drowning be inevitable, the easiest way to die would be to suck water into the lungs by a powerful inspiration as soon as one went beneath the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as practical advice for reducing suffering in shipwreck scenarios, based on the physiological argument that filling lungs with water brings on immediate anaesthesia-like insensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value diversity of pursuits for a mutual-improvement club
rubrics_metrics.description: The club should consist of persons of the most diverse pursuits—theologians, lawyers, physicians, engineers, merchants, and of all modes of thought—one condition only: that all be imbued with the spirit of liberal culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: general culture and contact with the best thought; diversity brings cross-disciplinary enrichment; science should be included among represented pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise inclusion of science in liberal culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the pursuits which ought to be represented here, none is so necessary as that of science; the spirit of science and the methods of science are more diverse from the spirit and methods of other intellectual pursuits than these are from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: science contributes unique methods and perspectives valuable for general culture and mental improvement; clubs should deliberately include scientific voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate scientific findings from philosophical inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution is one thing and materialism another and quite a different thing. The teachings of science must be distinguished from inferences of philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational principle: avoid conflating empirical scientific explanations (processes) with metaphysical conclusions (e.g., that evolution implies materialism). Teach the boundary so students do not attribute philosophical positions to science itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a life-culture sequence for education
rubrics_metrics.description: First, a general culture of all the faculties — a preparation for general efficiency without reference to any special pursuit — then a concentration of the thus strengthened and disciplined powers upon special professional studies (still connected with a scheme of liberal culture/university), and lastly, in active professional life, the formation of associations for continued contact with best thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-stage model for individual intellectual development advocated for clubs and education policy: general liberal training, professional specialization within liberal context, and lifelong associative learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek comprehensive views that reconcile partial truths
rubrics_metrics.description: In vexed questions there are three views — two opposing partial views and a third more rational and comprehensive view which combines and reconciles them; truth is often a stereoscopic combination of partial views, not a mere middle-of-the-road mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion for dispute resolution and philosophy: avoid naive averaging ('truth lies in the middle') and instead seek integrative explanations that account for both sides (illustrated by the shield white/black example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use science to transfigure and incorporate older truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The end and mission of science is not only to discover new truth, but also to give new and more rational form to old truth — the new must include the old, and the old must incorporate and assimilate the new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical stance: science should be presented as evolutionary and integrative rather than destructive of existing beliefs; avoid 'catastrophist' tendency to raze previous beliefs wholesale.
